analysis.title: Employment Situation: Job growth weaker than expected in September, keeping the Fed on hold in October
key_insights: September nonfarm payrolls rose 29k versus a 90k consensus. Prior months were revised down by a cumulative 60k, which pulled the three-month moving average of job gains to 51k.
PNC treats 51k a month as roughly the pace needed to keep the unemployment rate stable, because slower labor force growth and weaker net immigration have lowered the breakeven rate of job growth.
Private sector payrolls rose 46k in September. Weak local government hiring held down the headline number.
Job gains were concentrated in Education/Health Care (20k), Trade/Transportation (18k) and Construction (10k).

The unemployment rate was 4.18% in September versus 4.14% in August, which rounds to 4.2%. Higher labor force participation, not weaker employment gains, pushed it up. It has hovered around 4.2% for three months, in line with the Fed's view of full employment.
The underemployment rate fell to 7.6% from 7.7%.

Average hourly earnings grew at a 1.6% annualized pace in September. Six-month annualized wage growth slowed to 2.5%, below pre-pandemic levels, so PNC says the labor market is not yet a source of inflationary pressure.

Hours worked continue to strengthen, and aggregate payroll income is growing at roughly a 5% pace. PNC says slower wage growth with rising hours is a possible Goldilocks scenario for the Fed, and that a productivity pickup could reconcile this with Q3 GDP tracking above 3%.
PNC calls this a dovish jobs report. Absent a very concerning inflation print later this month, it should end the idea of an October rate hike.

PNC still expects the underlying labor market trend to be somewhere between stable and re-accelerating. It expects inflation prints to force at least two more Fed hikes, one in December and one in March.

The payroll miss was a surprise because higher-frequency indicators pointed to a firmer September. ADP came in above expectations and unemployment insurance claims improved markedly through the month.

Up from 4.14% in August on higher participation. PNC calls it stable at about 4.2% over three months.
Below pre-pandemic levels. The labor market is not an inflation source yet.

risk_factors: A very concerning inflation print later in October could revive the case for an October hike.
Seasonal-adjustment quirks and low survey response rates may be adding volatility to the payroll data.
Weaker net immigration and slower labor force growth have lowered the breakeven pace of job growth, so the same payroll number carries different implications than in the past.

tension_points.bull_case: The labor market may still be re-accelerating. PNC says the underlying trend is heating up and inflation prints will force at least two more hikes, in December and March.
tension_points.bear_case: The report lands in the stable camp. Wage growth is 1.6% annualized, payrolls missed by 61k, and revisions were negative, so an October hike looks unlikely.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A very concerning inflation print later in October would reopen the case for an October hike.
